# Learning Objectives

1.  Calculate probability of a [**sample mean**]{style="color:#E89543;"} using a population mean and
    variance with unknown distribution
2.  Use the [**Central Limit Theorem**]{style="color:#006a4e;"} to construct the [**Normal approximation**]{style="color:#006a4e;"}
    of the Binomial and Poisson distributions

## The Central Limit Theorem

::: theorem
::: thm-title
Theorem 1: Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
:::

::: thm-cont
Let $X_i$ be iid RVs with common mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$,
for $i=1,2,\ldots,n$. Then
$$\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \rightarrow \text{N}(n\mu, n\sigma^2)$$
:::
:::

## Extension of the CLT

::: proposition
::: prop-title
Corollary 1
:::

::: prop-cont
Let $X_i$ be iid RVs with common mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$,
for $i=1,2,\ldots,n$. Then
$$\overline{X}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}{n}  \rightarrow \text{N}\Bigg(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\Bigg)$$
:::
:::

## Example of Corollary in use

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: example
::: ex-title
Example 1
:::

::: ex-cont
According to a large US study, the mean resting heart rate of adult
women is about 74 beats per minute (bpm), with standard deviation 13
bpm (NHANES 2003-2004).

1.  Find the probability that the average resting heart rate for a
    random sample of 36 adult women is more than 3 bpm away from the
    mean.

2.  Repeat the previous question for a single adult woman.
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Example of CLT for exponential distribution

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: example
::: ex-title
Example 2
:::

::: ex-cont
Let $X_i \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$ be iid RVs for $i=1,2,\ldots,n$. Then
$$\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \rightarrow$$
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Seeing the CLT: waiting for the bus

::::: proposition
::: prop-title
1.  Set up
:::

::: prop-cont
Define the probability space and related random variables and events, including assumptions.
:::
:::::

-   Back to the bus from Lesson 13: each morning's wait is $X_i \sim \text{Exp}(1/10)$ minutes
    -   $\mu = 1/\lambda = 10$ minutes and $\sigma = 1/\lambda = 10$ minutes
-   **Random variable:** the [**sample mean**]{style="color:#E89543;"} $\overline{X}$, your average wait over $n = 30$ days
-   **Assumptions:** waits on different days are independent and all $\text{Exp}(1/10)$
-   The exponential pdf is very skewed, but the [**CLT**]{style="color:#006a4e;"} says
    $$\overline{X} \approx \text{N}\Bigg(10, \dfrac{10^2}{30}\Bigg), \quad \text{so } SD(\overline{X}) = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{30}} \approx 1.83$$
-   **Goal:** check this with a simulation, and estimate $P(\overline{X} > 12)$

## Seeing the CLT: simulate

::::: proof1
::: proof-title
2.  Simulate
:::

::: proof-cont
Run the simulation to generate outcomes according to the assumptions.
:::
:::::

::: columns
::: {.column width="62%"}

```{r}
set.seed(1124) # <1>
reps <- 10000 # <2>
n_days <- 30 # <2>

waits <- expand_grid(sim = 1:reps, day = 1:n_days) |> # <3>
  mutate(wait = rexp(n(), rate = 1/10)) # <3>

xbar_sims <- waits |> # <4>
  group_by(sim) |> # <4>
  summarise(xbar = mean(wait)) # <4>
```

1. Set the seed so we all get the same random numbers.
2. Save the settings: 10,000 simulations, each with 30 days of waiting.
3. One row for every day in every simulation (300,000 rows). `rexp()` draws one wait for each row, like in Lesson 13.
4. For each simulation, `mean()` averages its 30 waits. This is one simulated value of $\overline{X}$.

:::

::: {.column width="38%"}

```{r}
head(xbar_sims) # <1>
```

1. The first 6 simulated averages. Each one is the average of 30 waits.

:::
:::

## Seeing the CLT: summarize

::::: example
::: ex-title
3.  Summarize
:::

::: ex-cont
Analyze the output using plots and summary statistics like relative frequencies and averages.
:::
:::::

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}

```{r}
xbar_sims |> # <1>
  summarise( # <1>
    average      = mean(xbar), # <2>
    std_dev      = sd(xbar), # <2>
    prob_over_12 = mean(xbar > 12) # <3>
  )

sigma_xbar <- 10 / sqrt(n_days) # <4>
1 - pnorm(12, mean = 10, sd = sigma_xbar) # <4>
```

1. One row of summaries of the 10,000 simulated averages.
2. Compare with the CLT: mean $\mu = 10$ and SD $\sigma/\sqrt{n} \approx 1.83$.
3. The proportion of simulations with an average wait over 12 minutes. This estimates $P(\overline{X} > 12)$.
4. The CLT answer: save $SD(\overline{X}) = 10/\sqrt{30}$, then use `pnorm()` for the Normal probability. (The exact answer is about 0.138, because the sum of 30 waits is $\text{Gamma}(30, 1/10)$ from Lesson 13.)

```{r}
#| echo: false
prob_30 <- mean(xbar_sims$xbar > 12)
```

:::

::: {.column width="52%"}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot code"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5

ggplot(xbar_sims, aes(x = xbar)) + # <5>
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), # <5>
                 binwidth = 0.5, # <5>
                 color = "black", fill = "lightblue") + # <5>
  geom_function(fun = function(x) dnorm(x, mean = 10, sd = sigma_xbar), # <6>
                color = "red", linewidth = 1.5) + # <6>
  labs(title = "Average wait over 30 days (bars)\nand the CLT Normal pdf (red)", # <7>
       x = "Average wait (minutes)", # <7>
       y = "Density") + # <7>
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) # <7>
```

5. A histogram of the 10,000 simulated averages, scaled so the total area is 1, like a pdf (Lesson 8).
6. The Normal pdf the CLT predicts, from `dnorm()`, drawn in red.
7. Add a title and axis labels, with a clean theme and larger text.

:::
:::

## Seeing the CLT: sensitivity analysis

::::: extra
::: ext-title
4.  Sensitivity analysis
:::

::: ext-cont
Investigate how results change when assumptions or parameters of the model are altered.
:::
:::::

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

-   What if we only average over **2 days**? Only `n_days` changes (highlighted)

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "2"
reps <- 10000 # <1>
n_days <- 2 # <2>

waits <- expand_grid(sim = 1:reps, day = 1:n_days) |> # <3>
  mutate(wait = rexp(n(), rate = 1/10)) # <3>

xbar_sims <- waits |> # <3>
  group_by(sim) |> # <3>
  summarise(xbar = mean(wait)) # <3>

sigma_xbar <- 10 / sqrt(n_days) # <4>
```

1. Still 10,000 simulations.
2. The only change: each simulation averages 2 waits instead of 30.
3. Exactly the same code as before. Because we wrote `n_days` instead of typing 30, each simulation now gets two rows automatically.
4. The CLT's SD for $\overline{X}$ is now $10/\sqrt{2} \approx 7.07$.

:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot code"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

ggplot(xbar_sims, aes(x = xbar)) + # <5>
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), # <5>
                 binwidth = 1, boundary = 0, # <5>
                 color = "black", fill = "lightblue") + # <5>
  geom_function(fun = function(x) dnorm(x, mean = 10, sd = sigma_xbar), # <5>
                xlim = c(-10, 40), # <6>
                color = "red", linewidth = 1.5) + # <5>
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-10, 40)) + # <6>
  labs(title = "Average wait over 2 days (bars)\nand the CLT Normal pdf (red)", # <7>
       x = "Average wait (minutes)", # <7>
       y = "Density") + # <7>
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) # <7>
```

5. Same plot code as before, with wider bars (`binwidth = 1`) and `boundary = 0` so bars start at 0.
6. Draw the curve and the x-axis from −10 to 40, so we can see the Normal curve spill below 0, where no wait can be.
7. A new title for 2 days.

:::
:::

## 

::::: extra
::: ext-title
4.  Sensitivity analysis
:::

::: ext-cont
Investigate how results change when assumptions or parameters of the model are altered.
:::
:::::

::: columns
::: {.column width="38%"}

-   With **2 days**, the Normal curve is a poor fit
    -   Simulated $P(\overline{X} > 12) \approx$ `r round(mean(xbar_sims$xbar > 12), 2)`
    -   CLT answer: `r round(1 - pnorm(12, mean = 10, sd = 10 / sqrt(2)), 2)`

 

-   With **30 days**, they were close: `r round(prob_30, 2)` vs. `r round(1 - pnorm(12, mean = 10, sd = 10 / sqrt(30)), 2)`

 

-   Same code with `n_days` = 1, 2, 5, and 30 (right): as $n$ grows, the histogram becomes bell-shaped, just like the [**CLT**]{style="color:#006a4e;"} promises
-   The more skewed the $X_i$, the larger $n$ needs to be

:::

::: {.column width="62%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6.5

n_values <- c(1, 2, 5, 30)

xbar_by_n <- tibble(n_days = n_values) |>
  mutate(sims = map(n_days, \(k) {
    expand_grid(sim = 1:reps, day = 1:k) |>
      mutate(wait = rexp(n(), rate = 1/10)) |>
      group_by(sim) |>
      summarise(xbar = mean(wait))
  })) |>
  unnest(sims)

clt_curves <- expand_grid(n_days = n_values, x = seq(-10, 40, by = 0.1)) |>
  mutate(density = dnorm(x, mean = 10, sd = 10 / sqrt(n_days)))

ggplot(xbar_by_n, aes(x = xbar)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 binwidth = 1, boundary = 0,
                 color = "black", fill = "lightblue") +
  geom_line(data = clt_curves, aes(x = x, y = density),
            color = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ n_days, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(n_days = \(n) paste("n_days =", n))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-10, 40)) +
  labs(x = "Average wait (minutes)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20)
```

:::
:::

## CLT for Discrete RVs

::: columns
::: {.column width="49.5%"}
1.  [**Binomial RVs**]{style="color:#F08897"}: Let $X \sim \text{Binomial}(n,p)$

    -   $X = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$, where $X_i$ are iid
        $\text{Bernoulli}(p)$
    -   Rule of thumb: $np\geq10$ and $n(1-p)\geq 10$ to use [**Normal approximation**]{style="color:#006a4e;"}
:::

::: {.column width="1%"}
:::

::: {.column width="49.5%"}
2.  [**Poisson RVs**]{style="color:#6B8CC4"}: Let $X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$

    -   $X = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$, where $X_i$ are iid
        $\text{Poisson}(\lambda/n)$
    -   Recall from [Lesson 15](../15_Discrete_RVs/15_Discrete_RVs.qmd) that if
        $X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)$ and $X_i$ independent, then
        $\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i)$
    -   Rule of thumb: $\lambda \geq10$ to use Normal approximation

:::
:::

## Larger example (1/7) {.smaller}

::: example
::: ex-title
Example 3
:::

::: ex-cont
Suppose that the probability of developing a specific type of breast
cancer in women aged 40-49 is 0.001. Assume the occurrences of cancer
are independent. Suppose you have data from a random sample of 20,000
women aged 40-49.

1.  How many of the 20,000 women would you expect to develop this type
    of breast cancer, and what is the standard deviation?

2.  Find the **exact** probability that more than 15 of the 20,000 women
    will develop this type of breast cancer.

3.  Use the CLT to find the **approximate** probability that more than
    15 of the 20,000 women will develop this type of breast cancer.

4.  Use the CLT to approximate the following probabilities, where $X$ is
    the number of women that will develop this type of breast cancer.

    a.  $\mathbb{P}(15 \leq X \leq 22)$

    b.  $\mathbb{P}(X > 20)$

    c.  $\mathbb{P}(X < 20)$

5.  Find the **approximate** probability that more than 15 of the 20,000
    women will develop this type of breast cancer—not using the CLT!

6.  Use the CLT to approximate the approximate probability in the
    previous question!
:::
:::
